card.chief_complaint: found on floor, no memory, no prodrome

ask.changes_what: Positive: treat as probable arrhythmic syncope - ECG, monitoring, consider admission. Negative: supports reflex/orthostatic pathway only alongside other features.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of supine syncope to discharge a patient with structural heart disease, abnormal ECG, or exertional syncope.
ask.escalation_warning: Syncope while lying down with no prodrome should be treated as arrhythmic until proven otherwise - monitored bed and cardiology review.
ask.how: Ask what position the patient was in when consciousness was lost (lying flat, sitting, standing) and whether there was any warning (nausea, warmth, sweating, visual greying) or none at all. Confirm with a witness whether the patient was already lying down before collapse rather than falling to a supine position.
ask.negative_finding: Syncope only when upright with a typical prodrome favours reflex or orthostatic mechanisms but does not exclude arrhythmia.
ask.pitfalls: Sleep-related vasovagal syncope and situational syncope can occur lying down; patients may misreport position after amnesia for the event.
ask.positive_finding: Syncope while supine (like exertional syncope) was among the most specific historical predictors of a cardiac cause in patients with heart disease (Alboni 2001) and is a scored predictor in the EGSYS cardiac-syncope score; it scores against vasovagal syncope in the Calgary score.
ask.prerequisites: Reliable account of body position at the moment of loss of consciousness.
ask.rationale: Supine or seated syncope without warning strongly suggests an arrhythmic cause, which is high risk in this patient on sotalol with hypokalemia.
ask.title: Syncope while supine or seated without warning

ask.changes_what: Positive (prolonged confusion, lateral tongue bite): pursue seizure work-up (EEG, imaging). Negative with rapid reorientation: pursue syncope pathway (ECG, orthostatics, cardiac risk).
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on these features alone in patients with focal deficits, head injury, or possible nonconvulsive status; absence of tongue biting never excludes seizure.
ask.escalation_warning: Prolonged post-event confusion with fever, headache, focal signs, or no return to baseline needs urgent evaluation for structural, infectious, or ongoing seizure causes.

evidence.citation: Brigo F, Nardone R, Bongiovanni LG. Value of tongue biting in the differential diagnosis between epileptic seizures and syncope. Seizure. 2012;21(8):568-572.
evidence.population: Pooled: 75 patients with epileptic seizures and 98 with syncope from 2 studies
evidence.quote: sensitivity 33%, specificity 96%, pLR 8.167 (95% CI 2.969-22.461) and nLR 0.695 (95% CI 0.589-0.82)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical/video-EEG diagnosis of epileptic seizure vs syncope as defined in the included studies
evidence.target_condition: Epileptic seizure (vs syncope) - finding: tongue biting (any)

evidence.citation: Benbadis SR, Wolgamuth BR, Goren H, Brener S, Fouad-Tarazi F. Value of tongue biting in the diagnosis of seizures. Arch Intern Med. 1995;155(21):2346-2349.
evidence.population: 63 epilepsy-monitoring-unit patients with bilateral motor activity and/or complete LOC (34 epileptic, 29 nonepileptic) plus 45 patients with syncope (retrospective)
evidence.quote: Tongue biting had a sensitivity of 24% and a specificity of 99% for the diagnosis of generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
evidence.reference_standard: Video-EEG monitoring (epilepsy monitoring unit); syncope by clinical diagnosis
evidence.target_condition: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure (vs nonepileptic events and syncope) - finding: tongue biting

evidence.citation: Hoefnagels WA, Padberg GW, Overweg J, van der Velde EA, Roos RA. Transient loss of consciousness: the value of the history for distinguishing seizure from syncope. J Neurol. 1991;238(1):39-43.
evidence.population: 94 consecutive patients aged 15+ with transient loss of consciousness (41 seizure, 53 syncope)
evidence.quote: We found a seizure five times more likely than syncope if the patient was disoriented after the event
evidence.reference_standard: Eyewitness-observed clonic movements or automatisms classified the event as a seizure
evidence.target_condition: Seizure (vs syncope) - finding: disorientation immediately after the event (eyewitness report)

evidence.citation: Sheldon R, Rose S, Ritchie D, et al. Historical criteria that distinguish syncope from seizures. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2002;40(1):142-148.
evidence.population: 539 patients with loss of consciousness of known cause (102 seizures; 437 syncope incl. 267 tilt-positive vasovagal, 90 VT, 80 other)
evidence.quote: The point score based on symptoms alone correctly classified 94% of patients, diagnosing seizures with 94% sensitivity and 94% specificity.
evidence.reference_standard: Established cause of LOC (tilt testing, electrophysiology, EEG/clinical epilepsy diagnosis); split-half validation
evidence.target_condition: Seizure (vs syncope) - COMPOSITE Calgary historical point score (includes post-event confusion, tongue biting, head turning, incontinence items), not a single feature

ask.how: Take the history from an eyewitness where possible. Ask how long the patient was confused or disoriented after coming round (seconds vs many minutes), whether the tongue was bitten and where (lateral border vs tip), whether the head or eyes turned to one side, and whether there was incontinence. Inspect the lateral tongue for laceration.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of tongue biting barely lowers seizure probability (pooled LR- 0.70, sensitivity ~0.24-0.33). Rapid, full orientation on waking favours syncope.
ask.pitfalls: Brief myoclonic jerks and even a few seconds of confusion are common in convulsive syncope; incontinence and injury did not discriminate in Hoefnagels 1991. Tip-of-tongue bites occur in syncope.
ask.positive_finding: Disorientation after the event made seizure about five times more likely than syncope (Hoefnagels 1991); tongue biting is highly specific for generalised seizure (pooled LR+ 8.2, spec 0.96), and lateral tongue biting was 100% specific in Benbadis 1995.
ask.prerequisites: An eyewitness account materially improves accuracy; the patient's own recall of the event is often absent.
ask.rationale: Prolonged post-event confusion or tongue biting would shift the workup toward seizure rather than cardiac syncope.
ask.title: Seizure-vs-syncope features: prolonged (>1-5 min) post-event confusion, lateral tongue biting, head turning, incontinence

ask.changes_what: Positive: hold/adjust the culprit, check orthostatic vitals, ECG, creatinine and electrolytes; negative: pursue arrhythmic, structural, vasovagal or infectious causes.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not accept a medication explanation as final in patients with exertional syncope, syncope while supine, palpitations preceding syncope, known structural heart disease or an abnormal ECG.
ask.escalation_warning: Bradycardia or high-grade AV block, QT prolongation, symptomatic hypotension with AKI, or opioid/sedative toxicity with reduced consciousness need monitored care and antidote/withdrawal decisions.
ask.how: Reconcile every drug (prescribed, OTC, herbal, recreational) against the pharmacy list: antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-blockers, PDE5 inhibitors, rate-slowing agents (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCB, digoxin), QT-prolonging drugs, sedatives/opioids, psychotropics, insulin/sulfonylureas, NSAIDs/ACEi/ARB/SGLT2i. Note start dates, dose changes and timing of the last dose versus the event.
ask.negative_finding: No culprit drug or no temporal relationship lowers the probability of medication effect but does not exclude intrinsic cardiac or neurological causes.
ask.pitfalls: Patients omit over-the-counter, recreational and 'as needed' drugs; drug effects are amplified by age, renal impairment, volume depletion and drug-drug interactions, so a long-standing drug can still be the cause after a change elsewhere. Attributing syncope to drugs without ECG review can miss conduction disease unmasked by the drug.
ask.positive_finding: A new or up-titrated vasoactive, rate-slowing, sedative or diuretic drug (or an intercurrent illness reducing intake/clearance) temporally linked to the event supports drug-induced orthostatic hypotension, bradyarrhythmia, hypovolemia/AKI or delirium.
ask.prerequisites: Access to an accurate medication list (pharmacy fill data, carer, containers); ask specifically about new drugs and dose escalations within the past 2-4 weeks.
ask.rationale: Reviewing medications is crucial since sotalol and other drugs can precipitate arrhythmias or hypotension-related syncope.
ask.title: Antihypertensive / sedative / new-medication review (timing of last doses)

ask.changes_what: Positive: obtain 12-lead ECG scrutinised for QT, Brugada, pre-excitation and hypertrophy, echocardiography, and cardiology/genetics referral; treat syncope as cardiac until proven otherwise.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not discharge a patient with syncope plus family history of sudden death on the basis of a normal single ECG alone.
ask.escalation_warning: Exertional syncope, syncope with palpitations, or an abnormal ECG in a patient with this family history requires monitored admission and urgent cardiology review.
ask.how: Ask specifically whether any first- or second-degree relative died suddenly or unexpectedly before age 50 (including drowning, single-vehicle crash, SIDS, unexplained epilepsy death), or has a diagnosed cardiomyopathy, long QT, Brugada, ARVC or an implanted defibrillator. Draw a three-generation pedigree when positive.
ask.negative_finding: A negative family history does not exclude cardiac syncope; most inherited-arrhythmia deaths have no recognised family history and de novo disease is common.
ask.pitfalls: Families under-report and mislabel deaths (drowning, crashes, 'heart attack'), and many index events occur in relatives never evaluated. The finding is a risk marker for underlying disease, not a test for the cause of a given syncopal episode.
ask.positive_finding: A family history of premature sudden death or inherited heart disease is a high-risk feature in syncope guidelines (ESC 2018, ACC/AHA/HRS 2017) that shifts the differential toward arrhythmic or structural causes such as HCM, long QT or Brugada and argues for admission/monitoring.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or family able to recall relatives' health; verify with records when possible.
ask.rationale: A family history of sudden cardiac death would escalate the urgency for cardiac monitoring and specialist input.
ask.title: Family history of sudden cardiac death <50 y or inherited cardiomyopathy/channelopathy

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant hypovolemia/bleeding or medication-related OH and act; negative: large blood loss unlikely, but moderate loss still possible.
examine.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is frankly hypotensive, has an unstable spine/pelvis, or cannot safely bear weight.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing measurements in a patient who is already hypotensive, too dizzy or weak to stand safely, or has an unstable spine or pelvis; a patient too dizzy to stand counts as a positive test.
examine.escalation_warning: A positive test in a patient with possible bleeding indicates large volume loss and should trigger resuscitation and source search, not observation.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.target_condition: Large acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.target_condition: Moderate acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy
evidence.quote: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent, even after up to 1150 mL of blood loss (sensitivity, 33%; 95% CI, 21%-47%, for supine hypotension)
evidence.target_condition: Blood loss up to 1150 mL - supine hypotension (comparator finding, not postural)

examine.how: Measure BP and pulse after >=2 min supine, then have the patient stand and repeat at 1 and 3 min (standing, not sitting). Record SBP fall >=20 or DBP fall >=10 mmHg, pulse rise >=30/min, and whether the patient is too dizzy to stand (count that as positive).
examine.negative_finding: A normal postural pulse response argues strongly against large blood loss (LR- about 0.03) but misses most moderate (450-630 mL) losses (sensitivity 22%). Normal orthostatics do not exclude hypovolemia from vomiting/diarrhea.
examine.pitfalls: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent even after 1 L blood loss. Beta-blockers blunt the pulse response; sitting instead of standing lowers sensitivity; mild postural dizziness alone has no proven value.
examine.positive_finding: A postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness is highly specific (98%) for blood loss and is nearly always present after large (>1 L) hemorrhage. In an older patient with syncope, an SBP fall >=20 mmHg reproducing symptoms supports orthostatic hypotension, though asymptomatic falls are common with age and medications.
examine.prerequisites: Automated or manual cuff, an assistant to steady the patient, supine rest of at least 2 minutes first.
examine.rationale: Orthostatic vitals can help identify orthostatic hypotension as a cause, but should only be done if the patient is safe to stand.
examine.title: Orthostatic vitals: SBP drop >=20 / DBP >=10 mmHg or pulse increment >=30/min at 1-3 min standing

Prolonged post-event confusion or tongue biting would shift the workup toward seizure rather than cardiac syncope.
Reviewing medications is crucial since sotalol and other drugs can precipitate arrhythmias or hypotension-related syncope.
A family history of sudden cardiac death would escalate the urgency for cardiac monitoring and specialist input.
